items.body: The title gives it away. ]ex(s)it(u)[ is a “concept album.” The cover photograph might initially suggest a bucolic collection of field recordings, but Leonardo Barbierato has other ideas. Birdsong is indeed one of the first sounds we hear, accompanied by delicate guitar plucking and live processing. From the outset, the surrounding environment enters into the performance alongside instrumental gestures, electronics and the acoustic properties of each location. Each of the seven Patchwork pieces functions as an individual study within a larger trajectory. Their subtitles — “margine” [margin], “l’ora di punta” [peak hour], “la mania del controllo” [control freakery], “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” [fragments of ecotonal friction], “infestazione” [infestation], “condizionamento” [conditioning] and “hauntology” — provide a loose conceptual map. As Barbierato explains in the accompanying interview, the recordings grew out of five years of site-specific performances, with the characteristics of each location feeding directly into the music. The album only came into focus retrospectively, when excerpts from those performances were edited into a coherent sequence. Throughout ]ex(s)it(u)[, electronics, acoustic gestures and environmental recordings continually interact, their respective roles shifting from one piece to the next. Barbierato calls this condition “eco-tonality”, describing the intertwining of ecosystemic and performative sounds and the fluid identities that result. “l’ora di punta” allows guitar melodies to emerge from and disappear back into circuitry; “la mania del controllo” frustrates attempts to impose stable order through heightened sound levels; “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” places different sonic ecologies within a rarefied environment; while the textures of “infestazione” proliferate across the acoustic field. The extended “condizionamento” reintroduces birdsong, which grows increasingly synthetic before giving way to a slow accumulation of density and abrasion and a roughening of texture. “hauntology” turns towards the residue left by sound, retrieving voices that seem to belong to another timeframe. For all the variety of its source material, ]ex(s)it(u)[ holds together remarkably well. Guitar, electronics, birds, voices, resonance and the acoustics of individual sites move in and out of focus across the seven pieces. Barbierato’s “eco-tonality” ultimately describes something quite practical here: a way of performing in which the sounds already present in a place can alter the direction of the music as it happens. photo by Devadatta “Sk!” Valmiki, 2025 To help us piece things together, we reached out directly to Leonardo Barbierato. Throughout ]ex(s)it(u)[, the seven Patchwork pieces seem to form a conceptual progression: from “margine”, where different sonic worlds first come into contact, through “l’ora di punta”, “la mania del controllo”, “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale”, “infestazione” and “condizionamento”, before arriving at “hauntology”, where what remains is no longer the sound itself but its residue in memory. Were these seven pieces conceived as successive stages of a single compositional journey, or did that overarching narrative emerge only retrospectively? At what point did you realise they belonged together as one work rather than as independent electroacoustic studies? The seven pieces belong to a single performative and compositional process that unfolded over the course of five years. At the beginning, I was interested in exploring the ecosystems in which I performed through improvisation. This led me to develop a series of site-specific performances entitled [in situ], where the aim was to engage with the place to the point that it could actively shape the performance itself, avoiding to treat the place as a backdrop. Initially, I had no intention of releasing this material. In a sense, doing so seemed to contradict the very idea of site-specificity on which [in situ] was based. Those performances were conceived as experiences in which listening was inseparable from the materiality of the place: its light, its physical presence, and the network of relationships and perceptions that define a particular environment. However, when I listened back to the recordings, I realised that publishing selected excerpts could open up another layer of meaning. I became interested both in the sonic interactions that had emerged during the performances and in the idea that these recordings would be heard in places completely different from those in which they were created. I was curious about how this displacement might reshape the listening experience. So, to answer your question more directly: although all seven pieces originate from the same artistic process, the overall narrative of ]ex(s)it(u)[ only emerged retrospectively, during the editing and listening phase. It was then that I recognised the trajectory connecting the excerpts, a trajectory that, to some extent, also follows the chronology of the original performances. Your background combines jazz improvisation with artistic research in ecology, and your current doctoral work explores the relationship between improvisation and cultural and environmental ecology. Listening to ]ex(s)it(u)[, I was struck by how the field recordings — birdsong, environmental ambiences and site-specific sounds — never function simply as documentary material. They seem to interact with instrumental and electronic sounds until their identities become almost indistinguishable. How do you approach this dialogue between recorded environments and composed material? Are you trying to preserve the identity of a place, or are you more interested in allowing those places to be transformed through the compositional process? While working on my PhD at the Conservatory of Rome, which I recently completed, I became increasingly aware of how environmental sounds and what we conventionally call “musical” sounds gradually overlapped and entered into dialogue. Interestingly, this was also something noticed by people attending the performances. In my research, I describe this quality as eco-tonality: a condition in which ecosystemic and performative elements become intertwined. In most of the pieces on ]ex(s)it(u)[, the environmental sounds are not field recordings added afterwards. They are the actual sounds that were present during the performances and were processed in real time through an electroacoustic setup. Only in a couple of pieces (“frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” and “hauntology”) I used dedicated field recordings, which were nevertheless recorded in the same environments where the performances took place. My intention was to place all these elements into dialogue without establishing a clear hierarchy between them. Ultimately, the project has both an ecological and a political dimension. It seeks to encourage a more attentive mode of listening and a deeper engagement with the ecosystems we inhabit. I believe that composition can function as a device that subtly transforms the way we perceive and experience the places we live in. In that sense, I am less interested in preserving the “identity” of a place than in exploring its transformative potential through listening. One of the most remarkable aspects of the album is its treatment of listening itself. By the time “condizionamento” unfolds, the music seems to have subtly altered the listener’s expectations: instead of following individual events, one begins listening to relationships, resonances and the spaces between sounds. Was this gradual transformation of perception something you consciously composed? More broadly, do you think of ]ex(s)it(u)[ as a work that conditions the listener’s way of hearing as much as it presents a sequence of sounds? I’m really pleased to read your observation, because it touches on something that was central to the project. Yes, the gradual transformation of perception you describe is something I consciously sought during the performances over the years, and later tried to recreate through the selection, editing and sequencing of the material that became ]ex(s)it(u)[. As I mentioned earlier, the album aims to influence the way we listen. This intention is rooted in the belief that aesthetics, ethics and politics are deeply interconnected. I believe that changing the way we listen can also open up different ways of thinking, relating to others and inhabiting the environments around us. However, I don’t think there is a “correct” way of listening or a predetermined ethical outcome. What interests me is the possibility that listening differently may enable each person to inhabit and relate to the world in their own way, according to their experiences, memories and ways of making sense of them. In times of social and ecological crisis, I believe that the possibility of listening and acting differently can become particularly meaningful. For me, this is where the political dimension of the work lies: in creating the conditions for a different mode of attention. Whether that change lasts for a few minutes or extends beyond the listening experience is, of course, something each listener will discover in their own way. The album artwork quietly maps the Patchwork pieces onto a series of specific locations — from Morra’s Studio in Asti to the Parco Nazionale della Maremma, the Mattatoio di Testaccio and other sites — suggesting that geography itself forms part of the composition. Combined with the recurring use of field recordings, this gives the impression that ]ex(s)it(u)[ is almost a cartography of listening rather than simply an electroacoustic album. How important was the notion of site in shaping the project? Do you see these places as sources of sound, as collaborators in the creative process, or as traces that continue to resonate long after the recordings themselves have been transformed? At the beginning of the project, I spent a long time questioning what it means to act in a site-specific way and, more fundamentally, what a place actually is. Each piece on ]ex(s)it(u)[ is an excerpt from a specific performance of [in situ], connected to a specific location. The geography of these places is mapped in the artwork, allowing the listener to associate each track with its original context while listening. I really enjoy the expression “cartography of listening” that you used, as it captures an important aspect of the project. Throughout this process, I always tried to avoid treating places as soundscapes from which to extract material to manipulate freely. When I used field recordings, they emerged from encounters with the ecosystems themselves: for example, through conversations and interviews with the communities I encountered in different locations, who often pointed me towards sounds, events or relationships that were meaningful to them. In most cases, however, these sounds emerged directly during the performances: the movements of participants, objects being touched or activated, birdsong, cicadas, wind, my playing and all the other sonic events that became part of the situation. This is central to my understanding of site-specific practice: a place is an entanglement of personal, human and other-than-human stories, relationships and forms of agency that actively shape the compositional and performative process. For me, a place is a kind of patchwork, where each patch (each element that contributes to its identity) follows its own trajectory and interacts with others, sometimes in harmony, sometimes in conflict, and sometimes with indifference. Through this work, I try to make these relationships perceptible on a sonic level and to reflect on them actively. In this sense, the place collaborates with and co-produces ]ex(s)it(u)[. It remains beyond the production of the work itself, continuing to resonate and transform through each new listening experience. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Leonardo Barbierato 的专辑 ]ex(s)it(u)[ 由七首 Patchwork 系列作品组成，源自他五年间在特定地点进行的现场演出录音。专辑核心概念是「生态音调」(eco-tonality)，即电子声响、乐器演奏与环境录音三者持续互动，角色在不同曲目间不断转换。开头以鸟鸣与细腻吉他拨弦引入，录音地点的声学特性直接参与表演过程。「l'ora di punta」中吉他旋律从电路中浮现又消融，「la mania del controllo」通过提高音量阻挠稳定秩序的建立，「infestazione」让声音纹理在整个声场中扩散，「condizionamento」将鸟鸣逐渐推向合成化质感，「hauntology」则转向声音残留，拾取似乎属于另一时间层的嗓音。尽管素材丰富多样，专辑整体连贯性出色，乐器、电子、鸟鸣、人声、共鸣与地点声学在七首作品中交替进出焦点。

items.body: “Mood Starters” is the result of a collaboration between Belgian artists Pedro Maras (BedouinDrone) and Marc Ceulemans (Brainquake). They share a common vision of music and the atmosphere surrounding it, which has resulted in this 11-track album, released on the Bulgarian label Mahorka. “Mood Starters” is all about atmosphere—a dark and unsettling mood that evokes a sense of mental anguish. Intense, sometimes overwhelming dark sounds alternately blast you away and carry you along on an imaginary deathbed. The album sits somewhere between Dark-Ambient and Cinematic music, while being spiced up with other Electronic music elements, including a brilliant closing track that opens a window onto IDM. Add a few highly Experimental tracks to the mix, and you get a pretty clear picture of what “Mood Starters” is all about. At times, the music feels almost improvised, which I find to be the album’s weakest aspect. For the most part, however, the tracks sound carefully considered, crafted with a vast arsenal of sounds, effects, and even field recordings. BedouinDrone and Brainquake seem unconcerned with genre boundaries, preferring instead to experiment freely. The result is a collection of strong tracks that conjure up powerful visual imagery. I can only hope the duo will repeat this experience, as this album demonstrates enormous potential. (Rating:8). Listen to “Cages”: Cages by BedouinDrone + Brainquake About BedouinDrone & Brainquake BedouinDrone is the dark ambient and illbient project of Belgian artist Pedro Maras, built around dense atmospheres, layered drones and a cinematic sense of storytelling shaped by themes of loneliness, memory and collapsing emotional landscapes. Brainquake is the industrial project of Belgian artist Marc Ceulemans, working with mechanical repetition, distorted textures, fragmented rhythms and psychological pressure rooted in classic industrial traditions. The two artists had never met in person before recording together for the Bulgarian label Mahorka, which released their collaboration album “Mood Starters” on June 5, 2026.

items._cn_summary: 《Mood Starters》是比利时艺术家BedouinDrone与Brainquake首次合作的成果，两位创作者甚至未曾谋面便完成了整张专辑的录制。专辑以氛围构建为核心，呈现出阴郁不安的心理张力，密集的合成器音色层与田野录音交织，时而爆发、时而绵延，仿佛在虚构的临终场景中游走。作品横跨暗氛围与电影化音乐之间，混入工业节奏与IDM碎片化的电子结构，实验性段落不时打破类型边界。整体编排虽偶有即兴感过重之处，但大部分曲目经过精心设计，声音层次丰富且具有强烈的画面感。两位艺术家对流派的开放态度使专辑在保持统一情绪基调的同时展现出足够的内部多样性。

items.body: Synapscape The Future Ant-Zen Synapscape have nothing to prove to anyone other than themselves at this juncture. Thirty years and fourteen LPs deep into their career, the German duo of Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep have earned the right to either reprise the scraping, break-ish power noise they pioneered in their early years or, as is the case with new LP The Future, give themselves license to drift from that brutal and uncompromising remit. Carrying on from 2022’s The Stable Mind, Synapscape’s detours from ‘power noise for power noise’s sake’ finds them revisiting many of the genres and periods which preceded the style. There’s the dubbish echo and squall of “Five Four”, while “Pick” and “Valley” both feature foreboding synth stabs and rubbery bass taken from vintage dark electro and reframed in Synapscape’s far more skitterish rhythms. It’s tempting to try to trace the origins of these fluctuations, but as was the case for many years with another German duo in Haujobb, one member’s constant stream of side and solo releases concurrent with mainline projects, in comparison to the other’s relative silence out of the duo itself, makes this a tricky proposition. Münch’s recent spate of work as neat_less, for instance, is not so far from the serpentine, funky lope of “Disappear”, but there’s unquestionably something in those tracks which in unquestionably Synapscape and nothing else. Is that je ne sais quois the result of Kniep’s quiet but firm hand, or just the natural result of the pair’s chemistry? Such questions are effectively academic at this point. Synapscape’s legacy has long since been established, and for those who’ve spent any amount of time with the records which built it, there’s an easy pleasure in listening to them rework and rethink the sounds upon which it sits. Buy it. the future by synapscape The post Synapscape, “The Future” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._genre: power noise / dark electro / industrial / electronic
items._cn_summary: Synapscape 第十四张专辑《The Future》延续了2022年《The Stable Mind》的探索路线，从早期的纯粹力量噪声框架中走出，转而回溯并重构那些塑造其风格之前的多种电子音乐语汇。专辑中既有dub质感的回响与嘈杂，也有来自暗潮电子传统的阴沉合成器刺音与弹性质地的贝斯线条，被置入Synapscape特有的碎裂节奏结构中。文章指出，这种风格游移既与成员各自的个人创作密切相关，又呈现出无法被任何单一个体作品完全解释的独特化学效应。作为一支拥有三十余年历史的德国二人组，他们有资格重新审视自己赖以成名的声音根基，而对于熟悉其过往作品的听众而言，这种重塑与再思考本身就是一种清晰的愉悦。

"Oort Cloud" (6:21) etheric/ambient atmospherics open this one--a long, slow development as Fender Rhodes, heavily-distorted guitar, heavy bass notes and chords, and synthesized "bassoons," "flutes," and other atmospheric noises slowly populate and fill the sound scape. Amazing that this flute is not real (or else it would be credited, right?) Nice diversion but not quite what I was expecting and/or hoping for from this band's third album. (8.667/10)2. "Vogon" (4:51) smooth Jazz-Rock Fusion that is more in the realm of what I was expecting--add the bonus of an appearance of the great theatric cabaret Jazz artist Claudio Milano to sing/recite in his Demetrio Stratos way the lyrics to a made up language that the Aether gang created themselves (inspired by Douglas Adams' Hitchiker's Guide to the Universe). I love the music! It's quite like that of one of my favorite 21st Century bands, UNAKA PRONG, from North Carolina. Much more sophisticated than the gentle/soothing-yet-dominant Fender Rhodes would reveal. Very happy-go-lucky and up-lifting. (9.25/10)3. "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres" (8:42) ambient electric guitar picking in a sonicsphere of lush reverb is thickened by the joinder of layers of keys and bass before orchestral drums and electronic keyboard and lead guitar enter to jazzify the music as if Andy Summers and Robert Fripp were together again playing with an electronica keyboard wiz. In the fifth minute things quite down as Andrea Ferrari's guitar work begins to lead the band into a kind of SONAR-scape of Minimalist Math Rock. At 5:20 then we move into a more spacious scape in which Matteo's tom-tom pattern provides the foundational movement for a jazzy Fender Rhodes solo and, later, a weave with Andrea Grumelli's heavily-treated bass and Ferrari's distorted lead guitar in the mix. The heavily-reverbed song ends with the instruments slowly dismantling and slowing down the weave, reminding me a lot of 4 AD's 1980s instrumental band DIF JUZ. Nice piece. (18/20)4. "La Mélancolie Du Petit Prince" (4:37) over/within Andrea Serino's classical piano ruminations the other instrumentalists add their tracks of untreated fretless bass, computer glitch sounds, and natural and unnatural percussion sounds. It's as if Eric Satie was caught in a sombre-yet-romantic mood playing a piano in an empty French chateau while a group of construction workers and electricians were doing restoration work in and just outside other parts of the piano's salon or grand ballroom. (I can't stop picturing Chantilly.) Or one could compare this to Ruyichi Sakamoto's 21st Century (or life-long) fascination with sound recording glitches--the work he did with Christian Fennesz and/or Alva Noto. Pretty and suitably dystopian for our times. (9/10)5. "Panta Rei" (8:00) more (a different kind of) piano-founded sound exploration: it's not always harmonically pleasing, always on the edge of being melodic in familiar Western ways, on the edge of being satisfying while never really hitting the "right" notes. It's reminiscent of 1970s exploratory jazz (think Keith Jarrett) and also Smooth Jazz (Ahmad Jamal) yet also totally pleasing--at least, until the fifth minute when Serino and Grumelli lock into a five-note, three-chord progression to support Ferrari's rock-jazz guitar solo (that reminds me of John Abercrombie, Sonny Sharrock, Larry Coryell, and Fred Frith channeling their most aggressive Jimi Hendrix and Ornette Coleman energies). The song ends with Serino's piano, all alone, gently tucking us into bed. Interesting--to say the least. I really like a lot of it, though I've never been a serious fan of the free and loose distorted guitar shredding that Ferrari uses here. (13.5/15)6. "Swerve" (10:42) thought this song opens with simple, straightforward (almost child-like) Fender Rhodes play, other tracks of synthesizer and guitars soon join in, taking the music into more serious realms. Soon Ferrari seems to be relying predominantly on a heavily-treated (reverb) guitar sound--one that reminds me of Eef Albers on Focus Con Proby's "Wingless" and "Orion" as well as the "infinity" guitars of Michael Brook and Dif Juz. By the end of the fourth minute the song has become a serious Rock-infused Jazz of the 1970s variety, even incorporating time signature slow downs and speed ups, swaying shifts into more stereotypic Rock stylistics while and before re-incorporating more Jazz-expressive sounds, lines, and motifs. Matteo Ravelli's excellent drumming plays hugely throughout this one as does Ferrari's lead guitar while Grumelli and Serino's work provides more of the foundational work to keep this one on the rails. The final motif (presented in slow down mode) sees the blending and turn-taking of all four instruments before Ferrari's last notes sound, decay, and slowly fade away. (18/20)Total Time 43:13As a blend of old and new this album stands out as an excellent bridge--one that feels experimental and exploratory while, as alluded to, also firmly expressive, even honorific, of old "classics." This alone makes it a remarkable album but also the fact of the use of totally fresh and original compositions to do so makes it doubly so. Though it's hard for me to say that I like or love this music, I do find it fascinating and I do, very much, appreciate the labor and creativity that went into creating it. This has been a fun and enjoyable album to take my time getting to know but I don't know how much I'll be listening to it once the year passes. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of genre- and stylistic-blending Jazz Fusion. The band continues to explore and progress and I commend them and urge them to continue doing so.

items.body: The history of mital-U begins well before there was a label to put on a record. In July 1979, Bruno Waser met members of the Lucerne band CRAZY at a Siouxsie and the Banshees concert in Baden. A year later, he produced CRAZY’s No Chance, regarded by mital-U and the Swisspunk archive as the first independently produced Swiss punk LP. The record preceded mital-U by sixteen years, but the encounter established the pattern that would eventually define the label: small-scale independence, personal relationships, and an interest in preserving culture that commercial institutions often overlook. Waser soon formed mittageisen, among Switzerland’s early German-language post-punk groups, combining guitar and bass with analogue synthesizers and drum machines. Their 1985 single automaten travelled considerably farther than their home country, receiving international radio play from John Peel. When mittageisen ended in 1986, Waser stepped away from the project, returning in the 1990s as mev2, or mittageisen version 2, where music became increasingly entangled with computers, animation, and moving images. Bruno W of mittageisen, 1983 That convergence supplied the foundation for mital-U. Its first website appeared in August 1995, at a moment when an independent music label having any substantial presence online was still unusual; the formal label and mital-u.ch domain followed in early 1996. Even its name carries several overlapping ideas. “mital” joins the German Mittag with “metal,” while the “U” can stand for You, Urban, or Underground. Over the next decade, mital-U issued mev2’s Geld-Arbeit, worked with former Grauzone member Marco Repetto, released Toini’s Electronic Biscuits, and participated in the Swiss Kult-Hits compilations, where Swiss punk and wave shared space with Yello, Kleenex/LiLiPUT, Grauzone, The Young Gods, and Stephan Eicher. By the late 2000s, however, another aspect of the label had become especially important: recovery. Between 2008 and 2013, mital-U released substantial remastered collections devoted to mittageisen, Grauzone, and the Lausanne trio The Vyllies. Master recordings were restored and digitized; photographs, booklets, unreleased material, and period videos were gathered alongside them. Waser has said that archival releases are undertaken with the bands’ approval, with trust and direct relationships treated as essential parts of the process. Across these projects, the catalogue offers several points of entry into Swiss punk, darkwave, and electronic music, each shaped by a different set of musicians and circumstances. CRAZY Lucerne’s CRAZY supplied the practical education behind Waser’s later label work. Formed in 1979, the group belonged to the first generation of Swiss punk bands, with a lineup that included vocalist Urs Knüsel, guitarist René Kaufmann, bassist Markus Tremp, and drummer Christoph Buri. In Waser’s account of the period, Swiss punk grew from frustration with bourgeois respectability and boredom, a local response to a movement whose methods could be adopted wherever people felt the need to make something happen themselves. The independently produced No Chance established that approach on record in July 1980. The later CRAZY (1980–1982) compilation gathers 18 remastered tracks drawn from the LP, the subsequent EP, and additional recordings, accompanied by a booklet. Its place in the catalogue gives the label’s post-punk history a concrete starting point: the bands, friendships, and self-organized releases that made the next developments possible. mittageisen Founded by Waser in 1981, mittageisen brought analogue synthesizers and programmed rhythm into contact with guitars, bass, and German-language vocals. Their self-titled debut, released in March 1983, helped establish the group within the early Swiss darkwave scene and earned Record of the Week recognition on the Swiss radio programme Sounds! The band’s name also carried a connection to John Heartfield’s antifascist photomontage and Siouxsie and the Banshees’ Mittageisen, extending Waser’s interest in the relationship between music, images, and political expression. By the January 1985 release of automaten / neues china, mittageisen had developed a more explicitly electronic, dance-oriented approach. The 1981–1986 Remastered collection, issued by mital-U in 2008, follows that development across 19 tracks, including six previously unreleased recordings, with a 24-page booklet. Further editions have kept individual parts of the catalogue in circulation, including the 2016 vinyl reissue of automaten / neues china and the five-track digital EP 1983 Remastered, released in 2024. mittageisen, 1982   Grauzone For many listeners, Grauzone will provide the most familiar introduction to mital-U’s archival work. The Bern group took shape in late 1979 around Martin Eicher, drummer Marco Repetto, and bassist G.T., with part-time contributions from Stephan Eicher and saxophonist Claudine Chirac contributing to performances and recording sessions. Eisbär, first recorded for the 1980 compilation Swiss Wave – The Album, brought the band international recognition, reaching the singles charts in Austria and Germany. Their brief existence nevertheless extended beyond that one song, encompassing material such as Raum, Moskau, and Film 2 before the group dissolved in 1982. Working with Off Course Records, mital-U restored and digitized recordings for 1980–1982 Remastered, released in 2010. The two-CD edition assembles 21 tracks and a 24-page booklet, including previously unreleased tracks such as the English-language Polar Bear and a live recording of Plastikherz. In 2011, mital-U also produced the first official video for Eisbär. Together, the collection and video place the familiar single within a fuller account of the musicians who made it.   Grauzone, 1980 The Vyllies Lausanne trio The Vyllies opened another part of Switzerland’s underground to international listeners. Ilona Prism, Ursula Nun, and Manue Moan met at the University of Lausanne in 1983 and began writing their own songs out of a shared concern about women’s place in the music business. Their first five-track release was recorded in Athens that December after an introduction through the Greek band Yell-O-Yell. Subsequent recordings brought cello, violin, and piano into their combination of synthesizers, bass, percussion, and vocals, giving their gothic and coldwave music a distinctive instrumental range. Across Velvet Tales, Lilith, and Sacred Games, the group developed a body of work that included Ahia, Whispers in the Shadow, and Now We Fall, before separating in 1988. Released in 2013, mital-U’s 1983–1988 Remastered gathers 29 tracks across two CDs, accompanied by a 24-page booklet. The label’s restoration work has also extended to Urs Egger’s video for Whispers in the Shadow, preserving the visual dimension of a band whose theatrical presentation was closely connected to its music. The Vyllies, 1985 mev2 and Toini Waser’s own mev2 project connects the label’s historical interests with continuing musical activity. Begun in 1994, eight years after mittageisen’s dissolution, it gave him a setting for further work with electronic music and video. The 1998 Geld-Arbeit releases brought Marco Repetto into the project as a remix collaborator, carrying a friendship from the Swiss punk years into techno and ambient music. That collaboration also informed Electronic Biscuits, released in 2002 and reissued digitally in 2022 as mev2 feat Toini. Raffaela Felder contributed voice, guitar, and electric piano, with Waser providing synthesizers and samples and Repetto joining him on remixes. More recently, mev2 has returned to mittageisen material through automaten (-6y edit) in 2023 and bestaendigkeit der erinnerung (v2) in 2025. These reinterpretations make the relationship between the label’s archive and its current work particularly direct: the same recordings can remain available in their original form while supplying material for new arrangements. Wire With Wire, mital-U’s interest in documenting post-punk extends into a feature film. The British group behind Pink Flag, Chairs Missing, and 154 is the subject of Wire – People in a Film, directed and produced by Malcolm Boyle and written by Graham Duff in collaboration with the band. Waser became involved through the project’s 2019 crowdfunding campaign and serves as senior executive producer, with mital-U working alongside Underground Head Films on production and promotion, including planned DVD and Blu-ray editions. The project draws on filming at Rockfield Studios and interviews with Colin Newman, Graham Lewis, Robert Grey, Bruce Gilbert, and Matthew Simms, examining the people and working methods behind Wire’s music. In a September 2025 update, the filmmakers outlined plans for screenings in 2026 to mark the band’s fiftieth anniversary, followed by a full release in 2027 for the fiftieth anniversary of Pink Flag. Those dates were presented as intentions, with the film still being completed. Material from the documentary has already appeared in Boyle’s video for 23 Years Too Late (24 Years Later Edit), unveiled in March 2026. The video accompanied the announcement of Read & Burn 03+, an expanded edition of Wire’s 2007 EP issued through the band’s own Pinkflag label for Record Store Day 2026. It offers an early look at the archival footage informing the film and connects that work to Wire’s continuing reassessment of its recorded catalogue. Beyond the Records Waser’s film work also includes an executive producer credit on Celeste Bell and Paul Sng’s Poly Styrene: I Am a Cliché, which premiered in 2021. Recent mev2 releases have also participated in EarthPercent fundraising, directing proceeds toward environmental causes. Now thirty years old, mital-U occupies an unusual position between label, archive, production house, and cultural workshop. Its catalogue moves backward and forward at once: restoring recordings from Swiss post-punk history while releasing new mev2 material, producing films and videos, maintaining an extensive online archive, and using revenue left after expenses and artist payments to support future projects or environmental and social causes. For Waser, preservation appears to be an active practice, requiring old material to remain available, contextualized, and capable of entering the present again. Follow mital-U: Website Instagram The post Celebrating 30 Years of mital-U — Exploring the Swiss Label’s Catalogue Through Grauzone, mittageisen, The Vyllies, and More! appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Mildreda started back in the 90s but remained largely unknown and underappreciated, eventually fading into obscurity—until Jan Dewulf breathed new life into the project around 2009. He has since released his third album on the Dependent label, and Mildreda continues to attract new followers. With this new opus—which can certainly be described as a conceptual work centered on the theme of ‘reality’—the Belgian artist unleashes his creativity across no fewer than 18 tracks. The conceptual nature of the album is also reflected in eight distinct, shorter “Reality Check” tracks. Serving as interludes or introductions, they feature pronounced Cinematic elements alongside an impressive array of sounds, effects, experiments, and the fragmented voice of French philosopher Albert Camus (best known for his novel “L’Étranger”). The remaining ten tracks clearly form the core of the album—songs that reveal the true sound and essence of Mildreda, offering a continuation of the style fans may have encountered on earlier singles. Mildreda remains rooted in a dark, obscure, and at times tormented atmosphere, all cast within a Dark-Electro framework. Industrial elements play a significant role, particularly in the percussion. Jan Dewulf has truly outdone himself, offering listeners an unparalleled experience defined by both complexity and efficiency. Certain passages evoke the genius of Skinny Puppy, though without attempting to directly emulate the Canadian masters. It is evident that Dewulf is a versatile artist who has experimented—and continues to experiment—with a wide range of musical genres. At times, the sound leans towards EBM, as on the formidable “Silk Skin,” which recalls the menacing atmosphere of Front 242’s “Moldavia.” Some sequences sound slightly less dark, yet simply fit into the overall picture. Jan Dewulf’s menacing, distorted vocals complete the experience. Two standout tracks feature notable guest vocalists. There is the already familiar “Virtual Goddess” with Johan Van Roy (Suicide Commando), but even more striking is “Rückwärts” with Constantin ‘Breñal’ Warter (Calva Y Nada)—also a fantastic track. Mildreda delivers an expansive, detailed, and polished album where atmosphere takes center stage without losing sight of its danceable side. I believe this record won’t need a reality check to convince anyone that it is a remarkable piece of work. (Rating:8½). Listen to “End Of The Line”: End Of The Line by Mildreda About Mildreda Mildreda is a dark electro/EBM project from Ostend, Belgium, started in the early 1990s before splitting up. Jan Dewulf resurrected the project in 2009. Mildreda released the album “De Laffe Denker” in 1996, followed after the 2009 relaunch by “Coward Philosophy” (2016) and “Cowards” (2017). The albums “Fire” (2020), “Reinvention Of Pain”, “Liaisons Dangereuses” and “I Was Never Really There” followed in 2021, and “Blue-Devilled”, “Devil’s Gaze”, “Prophecies” and “Friendly Fire” in 2023. “Realities” is released on Dependent and features guest vocals from Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando on “Virtual Goddess” and Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada on “Rückwärts”.

items.body: Danish saxophonist and composer Maria Dybbroe has fast established herself as a unique voice in contemporary European music. With her collaborative quintet Caktus, she fuses influences from various genres into captivating, improvisation-heavy works. On her third release with Caktus, the cinematic Øyeblikk , she blends her group with the Norwegian Jazz Composers' Orchestra, OJKOS, for six interlinked pieces of sublime beauty and depth. The album title means “moment”, and each tune has an ephemeral immediacy at its core. For instance, “Kalvøya”, inspired by an island near Oslo, opens with a pastoral segment of bowed strings and flittering of the woodwinds. After setting a meditative mood, the dual drums of Knut Kvifte Nesheim and Tobias Andreassen add urgency with their sparse beats. The interaction between the booming brass and the twittering reeds builds delightful tension that leads to a warm, poetic trumpet solo. The 15-member band weaves a dynamic tapestry of sound from which emerges Dybbroe’s yearning, incandescent phrases. Nocturnesque, shimmering refrains usher in the conclusion. Another track that bears the name of a location is “Fornebu”, a peninsula in Bærum, Norway. The clattering of percussion and the fluid clarinet notes are like a bird calling in the early morning hours among stems blowing in the wind. When the rest of the ensemble enters, they build a quasi-symphonic performance. This is best heard when the muscular trombones blow in unison against the clarinet’s tender melody. As various sections trade lines over percussive rhythms, a peaceful harmony ensues. Hence, it reflects the town’s perfect balance of architectural beauty and natural preserves. The melancholic “Det nye år” (The New Year) consists of long, languid passages from the horns with sparse accents from the drums. Hints of mysticism infuse the serene atmosphere as lone musicians play nostalgic and celebratory melodies. Guitarist Arne Martin Nybo weaves a haunting, incandescent ballad, followed by cellist Thorbjørn Kaas’ lyrical soliloquy. The rustle of brushes and cymbals, together with deep, resonant basslines, color the backdrop with muted hues. The music perfectly reflects the joy, the regrets, and the anticipation of another turn around the sun. Øyeblikk is a captivating recording with stimulating multilayered motifs. It is both thought-provoking and emotionally moving. It is a perfect example of what collective improvisational music should be: creative without pretensions and enjoyable without being pedestrian. items._cn_summary: 丹麦萨克斯演奏家Maria Dybbroe与她的五重奏Caktus联手挪威爵士作曲家管弦乐团OJKOS，呈现六首相互交织的作品。专辑名意为"瞬间"，每首曲目都带有一种转瞬即逝的即时感。"Kalvøya"以田园风格的弦乐拨奏和木管颤音营造冥想氛围，随后双鼓设置带来紧迫感，黄铜与簧片乐器之间的张力对话引出温暖诗意的小号独奏。"Fornebu"中打击乐的咔嗒声与流动的单簧管线条交织，强有力的长号齐奏与柔美的单簧管旋律形成准交响化的对抗。"Det nye år"以忧郁缓慢的铜管乐句展开，吉他手编织出难以忘怀的抒情段落，大提琴家紧随其后献上抒情独白，刷过镲片的沙沙声与深沉的低音线为背景添上柔和色调。整张专辑编织出层次丰富、兼具思想深度与情感共鸣的动态音响织锦，体现了集体即兴音乐应有的面貌——富有创意而不矫揉造作，悦耳而不流于平庸。

items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - David Virelles: piano; Reggie Workman: bass; Andrew Cyrille: drums. Recorded at the legendary Van Gelder Studio, Creative Inspirations marks the debut album by Trio Imagination, which pairs the instantly recognizable Cuban pianist David Virelles with the unique rhythm team of bassist Reggie Workman and drummer Andrew Cyrille. These seasoned foundation builders invited Virelles to join them for a sort of spinoff of Trio 3, following saxophonist Oliver Lake's retirement from performing. Virelles' " Unseen Mother I " opens the album in an atmospheric, highly cinematic way, with punctuated piano constellations, wet percussion, and bright, piercing metallic sounds. Workman's fabulous woody bass arrives gallantly as Virelles expands the harmonic texture of the setting. " Unseen Mother II " reaches even more hypnotic realms. Both pieces derive from a nearly two-minute sketch included on the pianist's 2012 album Continuum , which happens to feature Cyrille. " Universal Sketches " places excellent bowed bass at the center, with Workman extracting exquisite overtones within a big, resonant sound. He then turns to pizzicato while the trio dives into obscurity and obliqueness. It's impossible not to fall in love with the trio's impeccable rendition of Andrew Hill's " Refuge ", which, despite being presented in a more straightforward way, acquires a fresh and personalized style via its demonstrative 6/8 time signature. Virelles plays it beautifully, and Cyrille enjoys a brief solo drum passage at the end. Among the best pleasures on the recording are the delightfully percussive, Afro-Caribbean-focused pieces such as " Pétalo ", " Neves ", and the closer " Para Ti ", which come full of timbral expertise and rhythmic elasticity. With angular structures creating an aura of incessant rhythmic discovery, these compositions amp the abstraction and curiosity with both transcendent foundations and noble, vivid harmonic surfaces. The piano groove in " Pétalo ", a piece composed by Virelles specifically for this trio, offers a grandiose Cuban feel, featuring an expressive bass solo followed by outgoing piano impulses. " Neves " continues this intelligent, modern approach, coming out with significant Latin vibrancy, imaginative polyrhythmic daring, and intuitive motivic insight, while " Para Ti " is a typical Virelles exploration charted with a conspicuous melody over a rattling rhythm. Trio Imagination moves freely from notated to spontaneous composition with genuine passion, effortlessly generating striking contrast in tonal color. Creative Inspirations is exactly what the title suggests—an album that leaves us wanting more as its curious layers and blends linger in our heads. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由古巴钢琴家David Virelles与贝斯手Reggie Workman、鼓手Andrew Cyrille组成的Trio Imagination首张录音，在传奇的Van Gelder Studio录制完成。作品将维列斯的古巴音乐根基与自由即兴传统相融合，开篇两首'Unseen Mother'以电影化的氛围铺陈和点状钢琴星座展开，呈现出催眠般的抽象纹理。对Andrew Hill名曲'Refuge'的重新诠释以6/8拍赋予其崭新面貌。专辑最突出的特质体现在三首 Afro-Caribbean 风格作品——'Pétalo'拥有宏大的古巴律动，'Neves'展现拉丁活力与复杂多节奏的大胆交织，'Para Ti'则以鲜明旋律搭配紧凑节奏收束。三重奏在谱面与即兴之间自由穿梭，音色对比鲜明，谐波层次丰富，专辑标题恰如其分地暗示了创作者之间持续激发灵感的互动关系。

items.body: The twenty-fourth-and-final issue in the Split 12” Series happens to coincide with the anniversary of its parent label, as FatCat Records turns 25. Over the years, the Brighton-based label has been a touchstone in the release of quality modern electronica, and there’s no better send-off to the influential series than a split release featuring the angelically-warped music of Ian William Craig and the lesser-known talents of Estonian artist Kago. The Split Series has always been an essential part of FatCat’s output, and began life a quarter of a century ago. This release is the first to get the party started in what will be a year of celebration, and this kicks it off in purrfect fashion. 1997 was the year it all began. The Split Series was initially set up as a sporadic outlet for more out-there, abstract, and experimental sounds which would normally defy classification. Running in parallel with FatCat’s early output, the Split Series soon grew legs and traction, and has continued to grow ever since; it was only supposed to last for a couple of years, if that, but things have a way of continuing, and the series has now surpassed two decades. Over that period, the series has become a cult, collectible item, ‘accruing regular critical acclaim and a reputation as a gateway outlet for adventurous collisions…pioneering new sounds’. To date, the series has taken in forty-eight different artists and united five continents. Its aim was to curate high-quality, challenging…12” records that resisted easy classification and would continually shift. Creativity knows no bounds, and the Split Series has always gone beyond the veil, stretched itself beyond standard expectations. Always engaging, always challenging, but providing easy accessibility all the same, nothing else sounds quite like it. Quick-turns and surprises lurk around the corners; the music can feature sharp, rollercoaster-like bends and dips, and always pushes the boundaries of what modern electronic music is capable of producing. Split down the middle, the record consists of Canadian singer and composer Ian William Craig’s eighteen-minute ‘Because It Speaks’, and music from poet and singer Kago. ‘Because It Speaks’ zig-zags between stunning harmonies and outright decay, its higher, spaced-out zones recalling a nostalgic, amusement-park psychedelia and a pale euphoria, while its rougher textures attempt to drag its music back down into darker, no-go areas, where light has faded entirely, and the dying flames of the sunset seems to make things more sinister. Kago’s vocals have more of a sharper pronunciation, birthing strong rhythms of their own. Slim, hypnotic electronics are also in the vicinity, creating something truly original. The fresh air and the clear atmosphere helps distinguish this part of the record from Craig’s hazier, clouded sound, offering 20/20 visibility after the earlier perfume. On the surface, the two musicians don’t appear to have much in common, but this helps to create a stark contrast, and they both share a universal truth in the use of their voice, and the passion they demonstrate for diverting it, morphing it, and mutating it, until it takes on a new shape and a new personality. Tonally-different sounds live at opposite ends of the spectrum, separated from one another, but joined by a single record, and the contrast fits the stark black / white clothing of the series. Another admirable quality is its long-running promotion of unknown artists, the record divided between fresher faces and more established names, giving them a space and an outlet on a much-larger scale. This record ends the long-running series on an immense high, a series which, over the years, has contributed greatly to the expansion and exploration of electronic and experimental music. Residing in the distinctive aesthetic of the series – hand-drilled, numbered sleeves, and a stark black / white design – the record is available either digitally or in a single vinyl pressing of 500 copies. SPLIT SERIES #24 by Ian William Craig / Kago www.fatcatrecords.bandcamp.com
items._genre: experimental / ambient / vocal experimentation / abstract electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑是FatCat唱片厂牌Split Series系列的第24期，也是终章，恰逢该厂牌成立25周年。专辑包含两位艺术家的作品：加拿大音乐人Ian William Craig贡献了长达十八分钟的《Because It Speaks》，作品在高亢和声与彻底崩坏之间来回摆荡，上层音色带有怀旧游乐园式的迷幻感与苍白愉悦，而粗糙质感则试图将音乐拽入光线尽失的暗处。另一位是较不为人所知的爱沙尼亚诗人兼歌手Kago，其人声发音棱角分明，自身构成强劲节奏，配以纤细催眠的电子声响，营造出与Craig截然不同的清新通透氛围。两位音乐人表面上毫无交集，这种反差正是Split Series系列的精髓所在——拒绝归类，不断自我刷新，二十五年来已联合五大洲四十八位艺术家，成为冒险声音碰撞的重要出口。

items.body: with d’incise Recorded live in Switzerland, the duo Illogical Harmonies (Johnny Chang on violin and Mike Majkowski on double bass) team up with electroacoustic wizard d’incise on various recorded sound sources. All three musicians have a background in the international improv scene, and many of the hallmarks of the quieter end of that genre are in evidence here: gradual, tentative transitions, simple motifs, polyphony and a sense of interplay, and rough, sometimes gently abrasive timbres. Structure is present in a subtle way, tipping the music back and forth between very quiet to moderately loud, all with beautiful precision and control. Chang and Majkowski play with the difference in pitch between their two instruments, often leaving a big hole between the former’s high-pitched tones and the deep, woody bass of the latter. This helps retain the classic improv impression of dialogue or toing and froing between two performers, showing how much current improv is still very much about playing (in the sense of playing an instrument) and the exchange of gestures as it is about sounds (wasn’t it an improviser who eschewed the noun ‘music’ in favour of the verb ‘musicking’?). D’incise’s played back recordings tend to fill in this void between low bass and high violin, without dampening the sense of interplay too much. With the calibre of the musicians involved being as high as it is, however, this 40-minute set ends up being full of both lovely playing and great sounds — it’s not a matter of one or the other. The chromatic slides up and down at various points are a particular highlight, as are the gentle breezes of noise brought about by d’incise. Sometimes I’m left wanting just a little more to lift things out of the ordinary, but more often than not it’s enough just to sit back and enjoy some very good music.   Illogical harmonies with d'incise by Illogical harmonies with d'incise   Johnny Chang Mike Majkowski d’incise Insub.
items._cn_summary: 这张现场录音专辑收录了小提琴家Johnny Chang、低音提琴演奏者Mike Majkowski与电声艺术家d'incise的合作演出。三位音乐家均深耕国际即兴场景，作品呈现出该领域静谧一端的典型特质：过渡渐进审慎，动机简洁，织体对位丰满，音色粗粝中带有柔和的摩擦感。结构隐而不显，音量在极静与中响之间精确摆动。小提琴的高频泛音与低音提琴的深沉木质音色之间刻意留出空隙，营造出传统即兴中对话来回的质感，d'incise的回放录音填充这一空隙却不削弱互动。半音上下滑奏与轻柔噪声气流是专辑亮点，整体在高水准演奏与优质声响之间取得平衡，多数时候足以令人沉浸其中。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国裔肯尼亚鼓手Sven Kacirek与二人组Odd Okoddo（搭档Olith Ratengo）联合83岁肯尼亚东部传统dodo歌者Ogoya Nengo共同完成。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打击乐与套鼓为基底，将电子律动与传统人声交织，合成化的复合节奏层层渗入却不喧宾夺主。如《Bara》从廉价打击乐声起，逐步叠加4/4节拍、贝斯线与木琴质感，最终让电子与声乐融为一体；《Sarah》则以Ratengo主唱搭配Kacirek试探性打击，在人声高潮处引入粗粝失真强化张力。乐评指出，Nengo的加入使唱片扎根于肯尼亚传统土壤，而Kacirek的电子语汇则拓展其全球维度，形成文化互答而非取代的格局，让根源音乐获得前卫面貌，创新亦获得古老质感。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki乐队以自制乐器为核心特色，所有演奏乐器均由废旧物品改造而成，包括tassofons、tilofons、kitchenofon等自创命名乐器，其音准与音质在专业录音环境下依然出色。专辑延续首作风格，融合克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴及中东旋律等多种世界音乐元素，每首曲目对应不同的文化风格来源。乐曲中可见大量即兴段落，展现乐手演奏功底，乐器选择与曲式风格高度契合。自制乐器的概念本身即是对当代乐器消费主义的反思——音乐源于材料与创造力的结合，而非昂贵的工业制品。整体呈现一种跨文化、跨材料的实验性世界融合美学。

items.body: Poladroïd packs eight lean, muscular tracks with throbbing bass, fat drum-machine punch and just enough EBM grit to keep the whole thing moving. Lean, mean and mechanical Poladroïd drops this lean eight-tracker of electro industriana, fusing lino-friendly aesthetics with European body-music gloss and a distinctly modern tech-funk sensibility. The moods are taut and tensile, the bottom end throbbing in post-Moroder blasts while the drums come in big and fat, all Roger Linn punch and TR-909 muscle. The result is an album that understands restraint but never sounds restrained. “Norilsk” opens proceedings with clean-air funk and a diabolically wiry synth topline that cascades like digital waterfalls. Warm pads gradually move into the frame, adding color and perspective as the track develops into a convincing soul-and-machine coalescence. “Lyuberi” follows with straight-up EBM propulsion, its hard pulse surrounded by huge string synths that give the track a cinematic glow without softening its physical impact. “Leningrad” reveals Mr Droid as someone not inclined to follow the routines of the pack, bending familiar electro and industrial grammar into something more individual and elusive. “Sochi” twists and turns through helter-skelter synth melodies, constantly changing direction while maintaining its​ muscular rhythmic center. We are now only halfway through as Roentgenizdat—The Soviet-era practice of copying banned Western and émigré music onto discarded X-ray film to evade state censorship—begins its closing moments “Girls From Omsk” digs deepest into the groove, riding a simple, infectious refrain that becomes increasingly impossible to shake. “White Boy Funk” steps forward on a clipped rhythm and wiry bassline, its fogged-out strings creating a sense of pressure and anticipation. “Doomer” brings the industrial vocal miasma, gruff and ominous, with proto-paranoia steadily gathering behind the beat. Closer “Escape To Tbilisi” finally lets everything off the leash: a stomping, skewed belter that sends the album out at full mechanical tilt. Roentgenizdat is available on Roulette Rekordz. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — One of Radiohead's founding guitarists (and still member) Ed O'Brien releases his second studio album as a solo artist. I don't know any of the guest musician/collaborators but you can bet that Ed had his pick of the cr'me de la cr'me!1. "Incantations" (7:41) a single repeating acoustic guitar arpeggio provides the bed for 1:45 of Ed's folk singing. It honestly sounds like something from an early Roy Harper album. Other instruments, hand percussives and electronics, join in to move the music into territory previously traveled by the likes of DONOVAN and BJ'RK. Floating background vocals sound like Bj'rk's Inuit Choir on the Vespero tours. At 5:40 the percussionist(s) are joined by drums, electric bass, electric guitars, and keyboard atmospherics--which play out until slowly being faded out while Dave Okumu's bass and Ed's reverberating guitar notes continue to the song's end. Cool song! (13.875/15)2. "Blue Morpho" (6:18) another really cool atmospheric sonosphere created by guitars, wordless vocals, bass, synth washes, and, this time, full symphony strings. It's quite lovely--even moving: chords and multiple melody lines floating, flowing, shifting, morphing, and melding into one gorgeous textural feast. And the whole time I'm feel quite a little debt owed (or homage given) to George Martin and The Beatles. (Think of songs like "Blackbird" and "I Am the Walrus" as well as albums like Magical Mystery Tour.) Brilliant and beautiful! (9.75/10)3. "Sweet Spot" (4:10) double lines of picked acoustic guitar chords woven into one though coming from both sides of the stage starts out this beautiful, atmospheric and kind of eerie (like GRAVENHURST) music over/within which Ed sings both lead and backing vocals. I like the way the orchestra strings slowly move to the fore as Ed's lead voice sinks into the instrumental mix. Eventually, the strings (and, I'll assume, keyboard electronics) end up alone, finishing the song after everybody/everything else has left. Not as memorable as the previous songs but rewarded for the creative sound and structural tactics. (9/10)4. "Teachers" (5:18) a funky bass 'n' drum pattern is surrounded and permeated by eerie atmospherics. Ed's heavily-treated ghost-voice enters toward the end of the first minute, singing in a pleasant monotone for a minute or so but then it leaves, whereupon the bass, drums, guitars, and synths all seem to spread out into loose, adventurous swaths away from but still anchored in the main theme. The final minute sees the vocal choir sing, "open wide" before the instruments all stop or fade away, leaving only weird electronic noises to close out the song. (8.875/10)5. "Solfeggio" (2:36) guitar/electronic harpsichord chord perpetuated with sustain and arpeggiation open this before more layers of voice-originating atmospherics enter and steer the with an eerie yet unthreatening kind of melody line, repeated over and over before signing off with a final lower-register three-note sequence, all the while the glitchy electronica effects are increasingly present, even rising to a driver's position, like something from a SyFy Continuum soundtrack experience (think Au4's "Everyone Is Everyone [and Everything Is Everything]"). More genius song/sound making. (4.4375/5)6. "Thin Places" (2:19) flute, wordless voice, synthetics all woven together to create a kind of dream-like out-of-body astral travel experience. (4.4375/5)7. "Obrigado" (9:53) a very cool, almost jazz-lite rhythm track over/within which Ed & Co. deliver some pretty awesome atmospherics (as well as vocals). The reverse-delay guitar effects for Ed's guitar solo in the seventh and eighth minutes are only surpassed by the dreamy psychedelic soundscape floating and morphing beneath it (and, later, by the amazing wordless vocal tracks raging in the background--which I think one must attribute to Clare Torey-inspired Awsa Berstrom). Ed's ultra-cool voice reminds me of both George Harrison, Gadi Caplan, Donovan, and Harry Nilsson as well as, you know, Radiohead. Really a cool, amazing, and powerful song. A pleasure to listen to every single time I do. (19.5/20)Total Time 38:15It's weird how much/how often I hear core/key Radiohead sounds in Ed's music here. This leads me to feel strongly how important and integral he was/is to the Radiohead sound--to their music.A/five stars; a brilliant display of creative/innovative sound and song crafting that stands out as a masterpiece of extrapolated future music (as if Ed's projecting himself into the 22nd Century or beyond--or even another dimension). A modern musical masterpiece. Highly recommended. One of the best albums I've heard from 2026.

items._cn_summary: Radiohead吉他手Ed O'Brien的第二张个人专辑《Blue Morpho》延续了其乐队时期对氛围与电子声响的探索。整张作品以原声吉他琶音为基底，叠加手打击乐、电子音色与弦乐，营造出层次丰富的声音景观。多首曲目采用循环结构，通过电子效果处理的人声与环境音的层层堆叠推进情绪。专辑明显受到民谣大师Roy Harper、Donovan及披头士（尤其George Martin的制作）影响，但在声音设计层面融入了当代实验手法。歌曲之间在氛围与节奏上形成对比，从宁静的器乐铺陈到带有放克律动的电子段落均有涉及。整体呈现出跨界融合特质，将艺术摇滚的内核置于当代电子与古典弦乐编配之中。

items.album: FOURSCHER Festival 2026: a line-up built on affinities, not hierarchy
items.excerpt: FOURSCHER Festival returns to Club From Hell in Erfurt, Germany, on 7 and 8 November 2026, with nine acts spanning EBM, dark electro, rhythmic noise and ritual electronics: Snog, Black Lung, Individual Totem, Mildreda, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash, Polykoptr, KIFOTH and Manipulation. items.body: FOURSCHER Festival returns to Club From Hell in Erfurt, Germany, on 7 and 8 November 2026, with nine acts spanning EBM, dark electro, rhythmic noise and ritual electronics: Snog, Black Lung, Individual Totem, Mildreda, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash, Polykoptr, KIFOTH and Manipulation. Having attended the festival twice, in 2024 and 2025, what stood out both times was less any single performance than the combination of a carefully selected programme, an open audience and the sense that organisers Danny Hildebrandt and Andreas Schubert were personally invested in how people experienced the weekend. That impression carries into the 2026 edition, where the nine acts are connected less by genre than by a shared refusal to treat the existing vocabulary of industrial and electronic music as sufficient on its own: some dismantle it, some stretch it toward ritual or techno, some return to it after decades, and some use familiar EBM structures to ask questions that have little to do with genre loyalty. The clearest example is the pairing of Snog and Black Lung, both projects of David Thrussell. Snog works through legible structures, songs, hooks, slogans and satire, using the dancefloor to examine consumerism, obedience and political absurdity. Black Lung strips away that accessibility for harder, darker and more experimental electronic forms. Their FOURSCHER appearances are billed as their only European shows of 2026; a new Black Lung album, “Ordo Ab Chao,” is due shortly before the festival. Individual Totem bring an electro industrial catalogue reaching back to the 1990s, including records such as “S.E.T.I.,” “Mothfly,” “Kyria 13” and “Electrostatic,” with live appearances rare enough that the Erfurt date carries weight of its own. Mildreda’s context is more immediate: “Realities,” released 28 August, pushes Jan Dewulf’s work into a space where dark electronic abrasion sits alongside more emotional exposure than the genre typically allows, while retaining the project’s Canadian EBM and Belgian electronic lineage. This Morn’ Omina arrive in their thirtieth year with new release “Vestiges,” which frames three decades as continuity of practice rather than a retrospective; the project’s rhythm-driven material has always worked to alter a listener’s sense of duration and physical orientation rather than simply carry songs. Heimstatt Yipotash’s 2026 album “Abyss” draws on the physical conditions of the deep sea, pressure, isolation, cold and downward movement, as both imagery and compositional logic, moving between aggressive electro, rhythm noise and more cinematic passages. Polykoptr comes from the wider Amnistia orbit and the Leipzig electronic scene, presented here on its own terms rather than as an extension of that name. The Slovak project KIFOTH released “Artificial Territory” in June 2026, reconnecting earlier KIFOTH material with contemporary EBM production. Manipulation return after close to three decades, with “Feel The Same” remembered as a small club hit from the project’s earlier run. Line-up and practical information FOURSCHER Festival 2026 takes place at Club From Hell, Flughafenstraße 41, 99092 Erfurt, Germany, on 7 November (19:00-03:00) and 8 November (13:00-18:00). The line-up: Snog, Black Lung, Individual Totem, Mildreda, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash, Polykoptr, KIFOTH and Manipulation. Tickets are priced at €70 for the weekend or €40 for a day ticket; electronic tickets are available, with printed tickets held at the box office on request.

items.body: A short intro on "Sculpting Silence" The nature of art is to make you stop you in your tracks, to stop doing what you're doing and thinking, and to start using your senses, your eyes and ears, sometimes your touch and smell to be surprised, to be confronted with the unexpected, to admire, to see things differently. We will have a short series of music that we describe as "s culpting silence ", music in which sound is used like the black lines of a pen in zen art, a few strokes that capture the essence on a white canvas. And the first album in the series explicitly refers to the Zen concepts of ' Mu ' and ' Shin ' : " The term combines the kanji Mu (nothingness) and Shin (mind or spirit), and is often translated as “no-mind.” It refers to a state of consciousness free from fear, anger, or ego—where action arises naturally and without obstruction. In musical terms, this becomes a space where sound is not forced or premeditated, but emerges with clarity and immediacy ", we read in the liner notes. So the few strokes on a white canvas - on 'nothingness' - are like the ripples on a still pond, the barely visible effect of the slightest breeze. Here are some descriptions I found on the value of the colour 'white' in Zen art, comparable to silence in music. In Zen art, white is not merely a blank background or an empty void. It represents 'ma' (negative space), functioning as living breath, silence, and the infinite potential from which all forms emerge and return. The unpainted white paper or silk is an active, essential presence equal to the black ink strokes. Zen painting uses intentional emptiness, asymmetry, and abbreviated forms to point toward direct seeing rather than decoration. Blank space is not “nothing”; it functions as breath, silence, and the field in which forms appear and dissolve. Common motifs—enso, bamboo, landscapes, and solitary figures—teach non-attachment and ordinary clarity. I also found some sayings about listening. "Listening stops with the ears, the mind stops with recognition, but spirit is empty and waits on all things." "What is this mind? Who is hearing these sounds? ... What is it that hears?" "The quieter you become, the more you can hear." Now about the album. The cover art is bizarre, to say the least: a cigarette-smoking armour seated on a toilet in a hilly landscape. It's in bad taste in my opinion, and not because of the toilet, but also because it does not truly reflect the nature of the music. It's a surreal digital artwork created by Aki Karano (also known as Akis Karanos) a visual artist and experimental musician, based in Greece. In retrospect, it looks familiar when you see the likeness with the traditional Japanese drawings of monks contemplating the world, and also seen from the back. There may be a reference, or it might just be a coincidence. Admitted, the monk is not smoking and not wearing an armour, and he's contemplating a circle and not a square, yet it might be a more modern, more surreal rendition of the same experience. Now really about the album. Both Susana Santos Silva on trumpet and Vasco Trilla on percussion explore the boundaries and sonic potential of their respective instruments, creating ringing tones, whistles, droplets, swooshes, rumbles, gurgles, swishes and many more sounds without name or description. The album begins quietly, with uncommon sounds cautiously flirting with silence—touching it slowly and gently, as if aware of its fragility. The result is a kind of soft intensity, with no obvious path or predetermined concept beyond the simple act of producing small fragments of sound and welcoming their clarity, their unexpectedness, and the ways in which they interact. This is music that has nothing to prove. It does not seek to impress, move, or even necessarily engage a listener or an audience. It exists simply for its own sake: to be savoured, appreciated, and perhaps approached with the same state of mind as the artists themselves—with no attachment and no anticipation. Such an experience can only emerge from going beyond the expected, allowing the music to develop organically and naturally, as if arising from nothingness. Contrary to the liner notes, I would recommend simply listening, rather than reflecting while you listen. Let yourself become part of the experience. Be there in the moment. Both Santos Silva and Trilla are masters of their art. They share a remarkable sensitivity and an innovative ability to draw sounds from their instruments that are rarely heard, while employing a wide range of techniques and tools to sustain the listener’s attention. As with much improvised music, the album may surprise you on a first listen, but it reveals more of itself with each return. Be the music. Listen and download from Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Susana Santos Silva与Vasco Trilla的二重奏作品，以禅宗'无心'（Mushin）概念为美学核心，将声音比作水墨画中的寥寥几笔，在留白（'ma'）中显现存在。音乐采用极度克制的即兴手法，几乎不使用预制材料，强调声音在静默中的自然涌现与即时性，与东方哲学中的'少即是多'理念深度契合。乐评并未对音乐本身做过多技术分析，而是以大篇幅阐述禅宗美学中关于空白、聆听与无意识的哲学思想，探讨沉默作为音乐素材的潜力。封面采用超现实数字艺术，将坐便器上的吸烟武士置于山景之中，虽被作者认为品味欠佳，但与音乐内在的禅意形成有趣对照。评论文字侧重概念解读，对实际声响描述有限。

items.body: Childhood summers spent in Val D’Arzino made an undeniable impression on Davide Cedolin. The artist describes Friuli in northeast Italy as “Mountain people, feral animals, ancient trees, old crafts, lore, abandoned crashed cars, ghost towns, houses named as boroughs.” On Cjera Aʃìn, the artist performs a feat of alchemy by translating the memory, feeling and sound of the land into a luscious suite. The field recordings are crucial, plunging one into the heart of the remote area; the music fleshes out the narrative. At the very beginning of “Cedolins,” the cricket chorus declares its presence, making Cedolin the accompanist. His guitar work rests in the American Primitive style, warm and wooded, like a hike toward the shady glade portrayed on the cover. As the notes drop down, they do not intimidate; their function is to produce mystery rather than fear. The crickets continue to chirp at the end; this is their territory after all. “Poças,” the first of three long tracks, ups the ante with guest performances on hardy gurdy, shruti box, percussion and double bass. This time the first impression is created by soft rain and the call of a local bird; the piece develops into a thick drone, a mossy blanket of mood, the earth is sending notes through the loam. The players pull back to reveal Cedolin’s banjo, the rain still falling like the accumulation of years, reappearing in the next track with a slightly different timbre, like the memory of a different summer. This time cello colors the mist of memory, producing a wistful, melancholic tone. At some point we hear – or have already heard without recognizing – the artist playing “woods and bones.” The land creates its own music; Cedolin draws from its treasures to make more. The taps in “Cerdevol” could be bones; or the tapping of stones by the creek. The flow receives a generous allotment of time at the end, setting up the crackle of “Benaandants,” an extended work filled with accordion, synth and fire. Val D’Arzino is woven into the artist’s story as the artist’s story is woven into the woods. Echoes and reverberations populate the background of “Cjanâl,” but to the woods, the guitar is the more temporary sound. Warm, gentle narration introduces the final track, which at 12:18 is also the longest. Layer after layer rise to the surface, the artist exposing different facets to the light. In the sixth minute there arrives a softening, with leafy rustles, a slower pace and light percussion that swiftly dissipates to allow the notes to take center stage. The impression is like the region seen from afar, regarded in memory rather than in person, the scratching like notes on paper. In the tenth minute, the music disappears, leaving only scribbles of sound. One cannot pinpoint exactly when the album ends, just as one cannot trace the extent to which a memory can linger in the mind. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: field recording / drone / folk / ambient / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以意大利东北部弗留利地区Val D'Arzino的童年记忆为核心，将实地录音与器乐演奏编织为一套声音叙事。虫鸣、雨声、溪流、火焰等环境声响贯穿始终，构成画框般的自然底色；吉他、班卓琴、手摇风琴、shruti box、合成器、大提琴与低音提琴在荒野录音之上层层铺展，形成厚重而湿润的drone质感。音乐与土地之间形成对话，乐器退居为环境的伴奏者，记忆、传说与声音在胶片般的时间流逝中相互渗透。作品不追求清晰的旋律或结构，而是在氛围与质感中探索地方记忆如何被听见、被触摸。专辑延续了欧洲田野录音与实验民谣交汇的传统，对偏爱实验与世界音乐交汇的听众而言，提供了极具沉浸感的听觉体验。

items.excerpt: You won’t come back for me calling was an SOS one more stop for me one more stop for more There are songs about heartbreak that behave as though somebody ought to erect a marble statue afterward, and then there are songs like SOS, where Barcelona trio Low Blows seem more interested in the miserable logistics of having cared too much.
